A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same publishers' game, ranking functions, and central convergence theorem. Their complete main texts, figures, equations, and appendices are readable, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix B report original simulations comparing publishers' welfare, users' welfare, and convergence across ranking functions and game parameters.

after.justification: Section 5 retains original simulation results, while Appendix C adds regret measurements, a softmax comparison, and experiments with non-uniform, correlated instance distributions.

M1.justification: The publisher utilities, proportional ranking formula, activation families, and LRL-OFTRL updates remain unchanged. Section 4 and Appendix B.3 newly specify and analyze a commitment procedure: each publisher stops at its own horizon and thereafter plays its averaged strategy. This is an additional procedure, not a documented replacement of the main simulations.

E1.justification: Appendix C.3 extends independent uniform synthetic instances to nine truncated-normal scenarios with different correlations among initial documents and among information needs. This broadens input-environment coverage within the same simulated publishers' game.

E2.justification: The linear, logarithmic, and root comparisons remain. Appendix C.2 additionally evaluates exponential/softmax ranking against linear ranking in the same game instance, with beta = 10 in Figure 10. This comparator is confined to the regret diagnostic rather than the main welfare comparisons.

E3.justification: Appendix C.1 introduces fixed 100-round evaluations of regret normalized by the horizon and averaged across publishers; Figure 10 adds individual regret trajectories through 200 rounds. Figure 2 expands the publisher-count sweep from 2–10 to 2–100. Appendix C.3 adds controlled correlation settings. The main learning rate, distance, and equilibrium tolerance remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses examine regret sensitivity to game parameters and activation hyperparameters, failure of LRL-OFTRL to achieve sublinear regret under softmax ranking, and robustness to correlated, non-uniform instance distributions. The existing hyperparameter welfare analyses are retained and relocated, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions state 500 simulations per parameter configuration and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals using B = 500 bootstrap samples. The later version retains this reporting practice; no changed run count, seed policy, or statistical estimation procedure is stated.

E6.justification: The later version adds results for larger publisher populations, average-regret curves, softmax-versus-linear regret trajectories, and nine non-uniform scenarios. New findings include linear regret growth under softmax and slower convergence as the penalty increases under truncated-normal sampling, whereas the original uniform experiments show little convergence-rate dependence on that penalty.

T1.justification: The original equivalence theorem survives as Theorem 2. New material includes an explicit finite-horizon convergence bound, Proposition 1 and its proof for unequal stopping times, and Appendix D's equilibrium characterization and welfare lemmas. However, Equation (26) omits a chain-rule factor C_i, which propagates into the new equilibrium condition in Equation (28).

C1.justification: The abstract and central characterization, convergence, and empirical trade-off claims remain essentially unchanged. The introduction adds equilibrium-strategy learnability and subsequent deterministic play to the contribution account, developed under stopping-time conditions in Section 4.

C2.justification: The later version explicitly distinguishes average convergence from last-iterate stability, explains commitment to learned strategies, and discusses why observed softmax convergence need not constitute no-regret learning. It also revises the uniform-sampling and welfare-analysis limitations and adds regret–convergence and activation-function interpretations. Appendix C.3 nevertheless describes a slower-convergence trade-off that conflicts with Figure 13.

D1.justification: The later version specifies average-profile equilibrium stopping, supplies the softmax example's document vectors and parameters, and documents the normal distributions' covariance structure and scale. It newly states that source code is supplied in supplementary materials, whose availability cannot be verified from the PDFs. The stopping clarification does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

R1.justification: The later version adds Yao et al. (2023, 2024a, 2024c) and explicitly distinguishes earlier no-regret welfare analysis from Nash-equilibrium convergence. The broader positioning remains intact. Madmon et al.'s changed citation year refers to the same work and is not an added reference.

P1.justification: Most core prose and the six-section progression remain. Revisions introduce the PRF abbreviation, expand the SEO motivation, replace the main-text proof with a sketch and appendix proof, move limitations into Appendix A, and simplify the experimental subsection hierarchy.

P2.justification: The paper is extensively reformatted into the ICLR layout, with redesigned author presentation, typography, headers, and figure sizing. Hyperparameter Figures 5–7 move into the main text, with the linear/root ordering exchanged. Figures 8–13 add regret plots and multi-panel distribution comparisons; existing plots also receive revised legends and axes.

improvement.justification: The later version clarifies the stability guarantee, adds a useful stopping-time bound, and directly tests the uniform-i.i.d. limitation acknowledged in v2. Regret diagnostics and additional reproducibility information strengthen empirical interpretation. These benefits are tempered by the missing chain-rule factor in Appendix D's equilibrium derivation and the contradictory convergence wording in Appendix C.3, limiting the net quality gain.
